1_sitz.summary: This 1963 Beatles single sits in the early British Invasion moment, materially conditioned by post-war Anglo-American youth-market formation, the 45rpm single + transistor radio + television (Ed Sullivan Feb 1964) distribution stack, and the electrified pop-music apparatus enabled by the Neotechnic electrification wave [MUMFORD-NEOTECHNIC, DIS-ELECTRICITY]. MODEL-KNOWLEDGE: the specific proximate conditions — post-WWII British austerity lifting, the baby-boom teenage consumer bloc, EMI/Parlophone A&R + George Martin production, and the 7-inch single as the era's dominant carrier format — are not in the substrate list but are what actually bear on the text. The lyric's second-person peer-counsel voice ('you should be glad', 'apologize to her') presupposes a mass-mediated youth vernacular that the electrification + broadcast substrate made possible.
1_sitz.tradition: Anglophone popular music (British Invasion / early-1960s pop song)

3_frame_axes.evidence_quote: 'I saw her yesterday' / 'she told me what to say' — the speaker relays what he witnessed and was told.
'Well, I saw her yesterday' — first-hand seeing grounds the report.
The messenger advocates warmly for both parties — 'you know that can't be bad,' 'you're not the hurtin' kind.'
No ultimate/world axis is engaged; the song stays within interpersonal romantic life.
The song's whole work is repair: 'Pride can hurt you, too / Apologize to her' — mending the relationship rather than dissecting it.
'Pride can hurt you, too / Apologize to her / Because she loves you' — reasons cited to motivate the addressee's action.
'With a love like that / You know you should be glad' — generalizes from the reported facts to a normative conclusion.
The whole song is about persons with intentions, feelings, pride, and love — 'she says she loves you,' 'you hurt her so.'
Reality is constituted by the triangular relation between she, you, and the messenger 'I.'
The end sought is restored romantic union — 'Apologize to her … she loves you.'
Reconciliation, repair of a rupture ('you hurt her so … but now she says she knows') aims at restored harmony.

4_moves.line_paraphrase: The friend proclaims the headline news: her love for you still holds.
The friend attributes to you the mistaken belief that your love is gone.
The believed content: you have lost your love.
The friend establishes his authority to correct you: he saw her, in person, the day before.
Contrary to your belief, her mind is oriented toward you.
She commissioned the friend as her messenger, giving him words to relay.
She says — in her own voice — that she loves you.
The content of her declaration: she loves you.
The friend attributes to you the recognition that this cannot be a bad thing.
The content of that knowledge: her loving you is not a bad thing.
The friend attributes to you the recognition that gladness is the fitting response.
The content of that knowledge: you ought to be glad.
She reported that you had wounded her severely.
The content of her claim: you wounded her, and severely.
The friend describes the severity of her past state: she nearly went out of her mind.
She now voices a revised view: she has come to know something new about you.
4_moves.move_type: reporting (assertion of her present cognitive state)

4_moves.line_paraphrase: The content of what she voices: she has come to a settled recognition about your character.
The content of that knowledge: you are not, in essence, the sort who wounds.
The friend attributes to you the recognition that the decision falls on your shoulders.
The content of that knowledge: the decision belongs to you.
The friend enters his own voice for the first time to venture an opinion.
The content of the friend's opinion: what is being asked of you is fair.
The friend issues a general warning: pride, too, can wound its bearer.
4_moves.move_type: gnomic warning (general truth deployed as pressure)

4_moves.line_paraphrase: The friend issues the directive that answers the standing question: make the apology to her.
